title: Managing resources, efficiency, inventories and lean production
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Manage resources effectively to produce goods and services, keep production and productivity apart, explain why businesses hold inventories, define lean production and its benefits, and show how efficiency can be raised.

blocks.heading: Managing resources effectively
blocks.text:
Operations management is the function that turns inputs into finished output. A brick maker outside Otjiwarongo combines clay, water, fuel, machines and the hours of its workers to produce bricks; a hair salon in Katutura combines scissors, mirrors, water, a chair and the same hours to produce haircuts. Managing those resources effectively means producing the output customers want while wasting as little of the inputs as possible: the right quantity, the right quality and the right timing.

The consequences of managing resources poorly are concrete. Produce too little and the demand that is left unmet goes to a rival. Produce the wrong quality and customers do not return. Waste material, hours or machine time and the cost of every unit rises, so the profit margin on each sale shrinks. Managing resources effectively is the foundation the rest of this topic builds on: productivity, efficiency, inventories and lean production are all ways of saying how well that job is being done.

blocks.heading: Production and productivity are different measures
blocks.text:
Production is the volume of output in a given time. Productivity is output per unit of input - the measure used most often is output per worker. Production counts the bricks; productivity asks how many bricks each worker produced.

Worked example. Otjiwarongo Brickworks produces 10 000 bricks a week with 20 workers, so productivity is 10 000 / 20 = 500 bricks per worker per week. Take on 10 more workers and production may rise to 13 000 bricks a week - but productivity falls to 13 000 / 30 = 433 bricks per worker per week, to the nearest brick. Total output went up while each worker produced less.

That is why the two measures are kept apart. A manager who watches production alone may congratulate the business on a record week while the workforce is being used less well than before. Productivity is the test of how effectively resources are being turned into output; production is the test of how much output there is.

blocks.heading: Why increasing efficiency pays - and how to do it
blocks.text:
Efficiency is the relationship between inputs and output: production is efficient when it achieves the most output from the fewest inputs, or the required output at the lowest cost of resources. Start from there and the chain to profit runs in steps. If output per worker rises, the same wages are spread over more units. Mechanism: the cost of labour in each unit falls, and the same happens with materials and machines that are used less wastefully, so the cost of each unit tends to fall. Consequence for the business: each sale now costs less to make, so the margin between price and unit cost widens - or the business can cut its price and try to win sales from rivals, because lower unit costs give it room to price competitively. For the workers who keep their jobs, an efficient business is more likely to survive and keep paying wages.

Two main routes raise productivity. Automation and technology put repetitive stages in the hands of machines, which work faster and more consistently than hand work and do not tire: a bottling line that fills and caps by machine out-paces any hand line. Improved labour skills work from the other end: a worker trained on the machine, the recipe or the packing method produces more or better output in the same hours, because skill removes the small errors and hesitations that waste time. Most businesses use both, and the two reinforce each other - a trained worker gets more out of a machine.

Neither route is free. Automation means heavy investment before a single unit is produced, and if demand falls the machines cannot pay for themselves; it can also frighten workers, and a workforce that fears redundancy tends to work worse. Training is slower and its gains walk out of the door when a trained worker leaves. A manager weighs the size and speed of the gain against those risks before choosing the route.

blocks.heading: Why businesses hold inventories
blocks.text:
Inventories are the stocks a business holds: raw materials waiting to be used, work in progress on the line, and finished goods waiting to be sold. The reasons for holding them come straight from what goes wrong without them.

Raw material stocks keep production running when a supplier is late or a delivery does not arrive. A furniture workshop that keeps no timber stock stops the day the delivery truck breaks down, and while the line stands still the wages, rent and machine costs continue - so a buffer of timber protects the business from a supplier's unreliability. Finished goods stocks let the business sell without a wait: the customer who finds the shelf empty often buys from a rival instead, and a business that can supply at once tends to keep its customers and its reputation for reliability.

Stock also costs money to hold. Storage space, insurance, the risk of damage, theft and deterioration, and - most easily forgotten - the cash tied up in goods sitting on a shelf, which cannot be spent on wages, machines or marketing. Holding stock is a balance: too little and the business runs short of inputs or sales; too much and it pays for space and risk while its cash is locked up. That tension is what the next idea, lean production, set out to break.

blocks.heading: Lean production: the idea, and how it is achieved
blocks.text:
Lean production is an approach that cuts every form of waste from the process - wasted materials, wasted time, idle stock and unnecessary work - so that only what adds value remains. It is not simply working faster; it is removing the activities and the stock that cost money without improving the product.

Two named techniques achieve it. Just-in-time inventory control orders materials so they arrive only as the line needs them, and produces finished goods only as orders arrive, so inventories sit close to zero and the costs of holding stock - space, insurance, deterioration and tied-up cash - largely disappear. Kaizen is continuous improvement in small steps: the workers themselves suggest and carry out changes to their own stage, and because the person nearest the work sees its waste first, a stream of small corrections adds up without heavy investment. A Namibian example of the spirit of kaizen: a Windhoek bakery whose packer notices that tarts are boxed in the wrong order for the counter, and re-sequences the tray so two minutes come off every run.

The benefits claimed for lean production follow from its definition: less stock to store and pay for, less material thrown away, less idle time, lower unit costs - and better quality, because a process stripped of waste exposes a defect at once instead of burying it under piles of buffer stock.

blocks.heading: Worked example: just-in-time at a bottler
blocks.text:
Oshikango Beverages bottles flavoured water for the northern towns. It used to hold four weeks of bottles, caps and syrup in a rented store. Moving to just-in-time means the bottle supplier now delivers each morning's crates the evening before, and the bottling plan is matched to the orders actually received, so the store is emptied and given up.

What changed. The rental of the store, about N$3 600 a month, stops. The roughly N$60 000 that was tied up in bottle and syrup stock is freed for other uses. Damaged and pilfered stock, which used to run at a few crates a month, has nothing left to damage or steal. Against that, the business now stands closer to the edge: a late delivery halts the line within a day, so just-in-time works provided the supplier is reliable and near - and Oshikango has begun keeping a one-day safety stock of caps, the one input with a single supplier, as insurance. The example shows lean production's trade in miniature: costs fall sharply, but the protection that buffer stock gave is part of what has been cut away.

blocks.heading: Three confusions to keep apart
blocks.text:
Production is not productivity: the error is treating a rising total as proof the resources are used well. In fact 13 000 bricks from 30 workers is more production and less productivity than 10 000 from 20. The test: ask whether the statement counts a total volume or a volume per unit of input.

Lean production is not the same thing as flow production: the error is hearing "smooth, waste-free" in both and using them interchangeably. In fact flow production is one production method among three, chosen when a single standardised product is made in very large volumes; lean is an approach to cutting waste that can be applied to any method, including job and batch. The test: ask whether the statement is about a method of organising the line or about eliminating waste - and remember that lean is an objective, flow a technique a business may or may not use.

Inventory control is not the same as just-in-time, and just-in-time is not the whole of lean: the error runs both ways. Inventory control is any policy for how much stock to hold and when to reorder - a workshop that keeps two weeks of timber as a buffer is controlling its inventory as surely as one that keeps almost none. Just-in-time is one such policy, the lean one, in which materials arrive as the line needs them and stock sits close to zero, and it works provided suppliers are reliable and near. In turn, just-in-time is one named lean technique, and Kaizen - small, continuous improvements by the workers - is the other the syllabus names; a business can hold stock at zero and still waste time and material. The test: ask whether the statement names one stock policy, one lean technique, or the whole approach.

Flow production is not batch production at a bigger size: the error is imagining that batch runs simply grow into a flow line as volume rises. In fact flow has no runs and no resets - one product moves without stopping - whereas batch is defined by the reset between groups; a fault is also felt differently, because batch loses one run while flow can lose the line. The test: ask whether the line ever stops to change over.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: This topic measures how well resources become output; the next ones price and locate that output. Topic 4.2 puts money on the ideas here - unit cost is what efficiency and lean production push down, and inventory decisions feed straight into working capital and cash flow. Topic 4.3 takes the quality side: consistent output is what automation and standardised methods buy. Inventory costs also return in topic 5.1 as a use of working capital, and the efficiency of a process is central to choosing between internal and external production in 4.4's neighbours.
